articles.title: Trump gatecrashed a NASA press conference after SpaceX launched a $4.3 billion space telescope
articles.summary: President Donald Trump phoned NASA boss Jared Isaacman during a press conference, saying the SpaceX launch looked "beautiful on television."
articles._body: SpaceX's Falcon Heavy is one of the most powerful rockets on the planet. Joel Kowsky/NASA via Getty Images President Donald Trump dialed in to a NASA press conference after the launch of a new space telescope. Trump called NASA chief Jared Isaacman and said the launch looked "beautiful on television." The Nancy Grace Roman telescope, which will study dark matter and energy, launched aboard a SpaceX rocket. Hours after a NASA mission to unravel the secrets of the universe blasted off on SpaceX's most powerful rocket, the agency's chief got a surprise call. President Donald Trump gatecrashed a NASA press conference after the agency successfully launched a $4.3 billion deep space telescope aboard a SpaceX rocket. The president called NASA administrator Jared Isaacman and addressed reporters and NASA staff to congratulate them on the launch of the Nancy Grace Roman space telescope. "Jared's doing a fantastic job, you are doing a fantastic job — and I'm supplying you all that money," Trump said, adding that the launch looked "beautiful on television." The President of the United States called into the NASA press conference after the historic Roman Telescope launch. There is a reason nearly 70% of Americans support NASA's return to the Moon, compared with just 35% during the Kennedy era. The world’s most accomplished space… pic.twitter.com/6100Nsl0dK — NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman (@NASAAdmin) August 30, 2026 The Nancy Grace Roman telescope, which has been in development for over a decade, is designed to hunt for dark matter and dark energy , mysterious forces that physicists believe play a vital role in shaping the structure of the universe. The telescope also features specialist tools that will allow it to block out the light of distant stars to directly view exoplanets, worlds in other solar systems that could have suitable conditions to harbor alien life. The telescope is on its way to an orbit one million miles from Earth after launching from Cape Canaveral aboard SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket. Falcon Heavy lifts off from pad 39A in Florida for the 13th time! pic.twitter.com/qh63XvOVtV — SpaceX (@SpaceX) August 30, 2026 Calling into a NASA press conference is the latest sign of Trump's growing interest in the US presence in space. The president signed an executive order earlier this month targeting an increase in the number of rocket launches to 1,000 a year, and last week announced a US space academy to train new NASA astronauts and engineers. The creation of the academy will be overseen by Isaacman, the billionaire and former SpaceX astronaut who became NASA administrator in December, and comes as the agency races to return US astronauts to the moon before the end of the decade. Trump has not always been so supportive of NASA's scientific missions. The president proposed budget cuts last year that could have led to the Roman space telescope's cancellation had they not been rejected by Congress. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: At Nike's NYC street race, where runners went head-to-head for rent money, affordability was top of mind
articles.summary: Some racers and spectators said $4,000 doesn't go far enough in New York's housing market.
articles._body: Akinola Raymond, 32, of Manhattan, grinning at the podium on Saturday. Raymond said his rent was $3,800 a month. Truman Dickerson / Business Insider Nike offered two NYC street-race winners up to $4,000 each to cover a month's rent. Some racers and spectators said $4,000 doesn't go far enough in New York's housing market. Affordability has been a major focus of Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration. Luckily for the winners of Nike's street race — and perhaps Nike as well — both pay less than $4,000 for their share of rent in New York City. The sportswear giant was offering that much, which it described as a month's rent, to two winners of a multi-heat street race held in New York City on Saturday. That's less than the median monthly rental cost for a Manhattan apartment. One winner, Destiny Scott, told Business Insider in a post-race interview that she lives with her mother in a "decent-sized" apartment in East Harlem. She said her share of the rent is $1,000 a month. "It can help out as rent gets more expensive ," the 26-year-old said of the prize money. The other winner, Akinola Raymond, said he pays $3,800 for a two-bedroom apartment in the East Village, meaning his winnings will just barely cover his next check to the landlord. Raymond said he lives with his fiancé. "We have a wedding in two weeks," he said, "so having that prize money helped us a lot." Saturday's race, held on Orchard Street in Manhattan's Lower East Side, drew dozens of runners willing to sweat it out in the late summer sun for a chance at winning some rent money. The race resembled a block party punctuated by bursts of activity as runners bounded down the pavement in different heats of 100-meter dashes and 400-meter relays. Hundreds of spectators lined the sidewalks and cheered wildly during the races. Nike billed the race as a chance to determine who was the fastest in New York, with the distinctly New York incentive of rent as a prize. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made lowering the city's housing costs a centerpiece of his administration. His signature rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments takes effect this fall, while City Hall is pursuing a broader plan to build and preserve 200,000 affordable homes over the next decade. The race came as Nike tries to recapture some of the cultural cachet it has lost in recent years. CEO Elliott Hill, a Nike veteran who returned to lead the company in 2024, has been working to refocus the brand on sports, rebuild relationships with retailers, and revive product innovation after years of losing ground to competitors like Hoka and On. For some spectators, though, $4,000 didn't seem like much given the cost of housing in New York. Favio Quizhpi, a 40-year-old police officer who lives in Queens, said the prize was a good incentive but that Nike was "lowballing it." "$4,000 would be nice, but depending on where you live in the city, that might not be enough," he said. Quizhpi said Nike should have "offered way higher." "They're Nike, they're a billion-dollar corporation," he said. "They can afford that." Astor Singh, a 25-year-old affiliate marketer who lives in Brooklyn, finished third in his preliminary group but didn't make the podium . He said the prospect of winning rent money appealed to young New Yorkers like him. "As someone in my mid-20s who's pretty early in the professional world still, it honestly catered directly to my life," Singh said. Singh grew up in Queens and Long Island before moving back to New York about a year ago. He said rising housing costs aren't an abstraction for him. "I have family out here who are getting slowly pushed out," he said, adding that he'd watched gentrification reshape neighborhoods he knew growing up. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: A gut health scientist who follows the Mediterranean diet shared his go-to, fiber-packed breakfast, lunch, and dinner
articles.summary: A gut health scientist follows a Mediterranean diet, starting his day with overnight oats and ending it with beans.
articles._body: Jordan Haworth is a gut health scientist. Jordan Haworth Fiber is amazing for our health, including by lowering the risk of chronic diseases like colon cancer. The gut health scientist Jordan Haworth follows eats 30 grams of fiber a day. He follows a Mediterranean diet, starting his day with overnight oats and ending it with beans. As a gastrointestinal physiologist —a scientist that studies the digestive tract — Jordan Haworth is well-versed in the ways fiber is important for our health. "Fiber has more benefits than just helping you poop," Haworth, who is based in the UK, told Business Insider. It helps lower cholesterol levels, balance blood sugar, and feeds the beneficial microbes in the gut. In turn, this can help lower the risk of cardiovascular disease, colorectal cancer , and diabetes, he said. Haworth, who is the author of "How To Gut Health," eats at least 30 grams of fiber a day, the official dietary guideline in the UK, and follows the Mediterranean diet , which is based on the eating traditions of countries including Greece, Italy, and Turkey. It is widely considered the healthiest diet in the world. "It's a set of principles, so it's like a checklist," he said of the eating plan, which centers on whole grains, legumes, fruits and veggies, and fish. He shared what a typical fiber-packed day looks like for him. Overnight oats for breakfast Haworth soaks his oats in kefir, a fermented milk drink. Jordan Haworth Haworth usually eats breakfast at work, which he prepares the night before. His go-to is overnight oats soaked in kefir, a fermented milk drink, Greek yogurt, frozen raspberries, a tablespoon of chia seeds, and some walnuts. At eight grams per cup, raspberries are particularly high in fiber, and just one ounce of chia seeds contains around 10 grams. Recently, he's started experimenting with soaking other whole grains instead of oats so that he's regularly eating a wider range of plant foods. "We know that eating different plants helps you to have a more diverse gut microbiome, and that is linked to better overall health," he said. So far, he's tried barley and buckwheat. Wholewheat Greek-style pasta salad Haworth loves Greek salad. Jordan Haworth For lunch, Haworth makes something simple. Yesterday, for example, he had a salad with whole wheat pasta, as it contains more fiber than its white counterpart. He added chopped cucumber, red onion, tomatoes, bell peppers, and feta cheese — the ingredients you'd find in a traditional Greek salad— and lots of extra virgin olive oil, an antioxidant-packed mainstay of the Mediterranean diet. A one-pot dinner Haworth always has a type of legume at dinner. Jordan Haworth Haworth loves a one-pot dinner. They usually contain a portion of fatty fish — such as salmon, mackerel, or sardines — and a legume, such as chickpeas or beans. "Half a can of beans is about seven to eight grams of fiber," he said. Haworth usually starts by adding garlic and olive oil to a pan, then adds the fish, legumes, and some vegetables, which he seasons with a variety of herbs and spices. He might have some whole-wheat bread on the side for extra fiber. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: I source meat from US ranchers. Here's why Trump's plan to lower beef prices worries me.
articles.summary: Ben Spell, founder of Good Ranchers, said the US should rebuild its cattle herds, lower costs for cattle producers, and expand domestic processing.
articles._body: Ben Spell is the founder of Good Rancher, Courtesy of Ben Spell Ben Spell cofounded Good Ranchers, an American meat and seafood delivery subscription company. Spell said beef is too expensive for American families, but importing more meat isn't the solution. He said Trump's plan highlights the need for country-of-origin laws on meat products. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ben Spell, the founder of Good Ranchers, a meat and seafood delivery subscription company that sources all its products from American ranchers. This month, President Donald Trump said he would allow up to 300,000 metric tons of beef to be imported into the US with no out-of-quota tariff over the next 90 days. Trump said he would also allow ranchers and farmers to process their own meat. The article has been edited for length and clarity. My wife and I started Good Ranchers in 2018. Before that, I was a worship pastor and worked at one of the largest churches in Houston. Around 2015, after a Sunday service, God just put in my heart not to take a salary from the church. I was like, "Well, what does that mean?" I had this idea to make a meat company. At the end of 2017, we just had our first baby boy, and I was getting ready for service. I came out of the bathroom, and I told my wife, "I think God told me to start a meat company," thinking she was going to go, "We just had a baby. We don't know anything about this." Instead, she said, "If you heard God, then I trust you." I resigned at the end of that year, and in February, I started selling meat out of the back of a refrigerated box truck. By 2020, we had about 20 trucks going around the country. We started shipping online, shut down all the trucks by the end of 2021, and went fully online. Our mission at Good Ranchers is to connect the American family to the American farm. Most of the ranches we work with are in Colorado, Utah, South Dakota, Montana, and Wyoming. We have some in Texas and Nebraska as well. While I hate the economics of how high meat prices are right now, I do think this is a wake-up call for consumers. When they think of beef, they think of a cow factory or a hamburger, but the average herd size of the hundreds of thousands of independent ranchers in the United States is only about 50. The price of beef has increased dramatically over the last five years. We've held our prices very stable, but we are at a tipping point. It's not a 90-day fix. Cattle prices need to be strong enough for ranchers to make money, and that's how you can rebuild the supply, but cattle aren't widgets. You can't turn a factory on and produce millions more cattle next month. Rebuilding the herd takes years, and if we crush the economic incentive to rebuild today, we're prolonging the supply problem we're trying to solve. I do think the president is correctly identifying a problem. Beef is too expensive for American families, but I strongly disagree that importing more cheap foreign beef with no transparency is going to fix the long-term solution. We need to make cattle production attractive for producers to rebuild the herds, reduce unnecessary barriers and costs for American producers, and expand the domestic processing capacity and competition. Imports I'm hoping and trusting that we'll get more information about the plan, but as that announcement sits, there's so much ambiguity. We haven't been told where the imported beef is coming from, how the cows were raised, what they were fed, what their health was like, or what antibiotics or vaccines were used. It would mean a lot if this could get a mandatory country-of-origin labeling law put back in place for beef in the United States. That would be a huge win for American agriculture. One of the biggest hurdles we have is that people don't realize that most of the meat they're buying probably isn't coming from the US. We're not saying that there shouldn't be imports because they do play a part in the system, but American families should be able to look at a package of beef and know where the animal was raised. Let the consumer make the choice of what they want to purchase. Processing The president's recent announcement is encouraging, but the details will determine whether it creates real competition or is a minor expansion on something ranchers can already do on a limited basis. Under the current law, ranchers can already use a custom-exempt processor for personal or household consumption, but that means the meat must be marked as not for sale. It needs to be processed under a federal inspection and an eligible state inspection program or a cooperative interstate shipment program. Federal inspection is required for interstate commerce. What Trump's plan could do is open up more processing at the ranch level. Earlier this year, the USDA announced a processor action plan that made $60 million available for expanding independent and domestically owned processing capacity. Hopefully, this will accelerate and broaden that network, which I believe is ultimately very good. This is not a political issue. It's an issue of food governance and food safety for the American people. That's really what we all want: high quality, transparency, and affordable prices at checkout. articles.title: Here's where some of the biggest labor unions stand on data centers
articles.summary: Some major unions have become Big Tech's allies in the battle over data center construction, even as the broader public rejects them.
articles._body: Some national labor unions are opposing AI data center bans and moratoriums in the US. Noah Berger/Getty Images via Amazon Web Services The AI industry needs electricians, plumbers, and construction workers to build its data centers. As a result, the tradespeople are commanding high salaries. Some national labor unions are now siding with developers in the AI data center debate. AI is both taking jobs and creating them. That's led to a divide among labor unions over AI data centers. And it largely depends on the kinds of workers they represent. The majority of the public is against AI data centers, according to polling. They worry about the environmental impacts, their strain on the electric grid, noise, or they just generally don't like the idea of artificial intelligence. Many communities have already taken action. A dozen towns in North Carolina have implemented moratoriums, and two have permanently banned the facilities. New York became the first state to approve an AI data center moratorium in July. Others are tightening restrictions. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott initially showed enthusiasm for building AI data centers across the state, but has more recently issued tighter restrictions on developers after backlash from residents. On Capitol Hill, Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Bernie Sanders have called for a nationwide moratorium. AI companies, which depend on data centers to power their products, have tried to stave off such calls by promoting potential benefits like tax windfalls and job creation (at least during the construction phase ). The jobs part is resonating with national labor unions representing electricians, plumbers, and construction workers. Unions representing workers who see AI as a threat to their jobs, however, have taken the opposite stance. Here's where some of the largest unions stand on the issue. International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers In April, the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers told its 901,000 members to urge members of Congress to oppose any bills that would ban data center construction. The union provided its members with a digital toolkit that included a sample letter to send to lawmakers and instructions for social media posts. "Such bans would eliminate critical opportunities for union workers and stunt much-needed economic growth in communities across the country," the union said. "When built responsibly, data centers mean high-quality union jobs, significant tax revenue, and long-term economic development." The IBEW said such projects provide its members with consistent work, high wages, and career opportunities. Don Slaiman, political coordinator of IBEW Local 26, which covers DC, Maryland, and Virginia, said in a recent op-ed in The New York Times that workers are already seeing the benefits of data center construction. "Our apprentices' starting pay is around $28 an hour. Experienced electricians earn $62 an hour plus another $30 an hour in benefits. These are union careers, not gig work, and they're open to people who might not otherwise have a clear path into the middle class," Slaiman said. Some people in the electrical field are earning high six-figure salaries working at data centers. Slaiman added, "Data centers represent the best opportunity in generations for blue-collar workers to attain a portion of the American dream." North America's Building Trades Unions Earlier this month, North America's Building Trades Unions, which represents over 3 million workers across the US and Canada, also weighed in. NABTU President Sean McGarvey called AI data centers "critical infrastructure that underpin America's digital economy, data security, and national security." In a press release, he applauded Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro for implementing new guardrails for data center developers without pausing or banning them entirely. "Gov. Shapiro's approach shows that clear standards, transparency, and accountability are the right and responsible way forward to ensure communities benefit, not the blanket moratoriums imposed in other states," McGarvey said. Laborers' International Union of North America One day later, the Laborers' International Union of North America also praised Shapiro's decision. The union represents over 500,000 construction workers. "Moratoriums on data center construction are not the answer," General President Brent Booker said in a press release. United Association United Association, a union representing around 407,000 workers in the plumbing and pipe-fitting industries, has also pushed for more data center construction. "Data centers are the essential infrastructure of the internet and everything we take for granted in our daily lives: cellphones, social media, Uber and Lyft, Netflix, smart TVs, online banking, ChatGPT, and modern-day life as we know it," the union says in a fact sheet on data centers that's posted to its website. The union also criticized New Jersey Rep. Frank Pallone's decision to support a nationwide moratorium on new data center construction. "For the United Association, the expansion of data centers means stable jobs and the opportunity to provide for our families," Mark McManus, the union's general president, said in a letter addressed to Pallone. He added, "A kneejerk moratorium based on misinformation is not the common-sense answer we need." National Nurses United National Nurses United, meanwhile, which represents almost 225,000 workers, says it supports Sanders' push for a nationwide moratorium. The union said it would put "nurses, patients, and working people in the driver's seat." The union's concerns are both about the impact data centers could have on communities and the wider impact of artificial intelligence on nursing jobs. "The moratorium will give us time to build enforceable protections into law to keep ourselves, our work and our democracy safe, and autonomy to decide how and if we want A.I. to impact our lives," the union said in its data center f

articles.title: I'm a Big Tech executive. My journey here has felt like falling forward — painful stumbles and detours, yet still progress.
articles.summary: Wainwright Yu reflects on his career at a Magnificent 7 company, detailing missed opportunities and resilience in achieving his success.
articles._body: Wainwright Yu. Courtesy of Wainwright Yu Wainwright Yu's unexpected journey at a Magnificent 7 company led to a director role, despite setbacks. Not landing a return offer after an internship and unexpected team assignments were part of his journey. Yu said what he had to let go of was the perfect career path he had crafted in his head. The email came in on a Tuesday. It was an announcement that I had been promoted to director, an executive position at the Magnificent 7 company, where I had worked for eight years. Follow-up congratulatory emails started to pour in. I sent brief but genuine replies, "Thank you." A few weeks later, another email went out. My manager was leaving the team. Having just been promoted, I thought this was an obvious next step for me. That didn't happen. They were hiring someone else instead — another director from another team was coming in to take his place. My role and title stayed intact, but there was no scope expansion for me. I earned the title, but I didn't have what I thought it signified: readiness for more. From the outside, a career at a Magnificent 7 company looks like a straight line — competitive offer, steady promotions, increasing scope. From the inside, it rarely feels that way. Mine certainly didn't. What it felt like, more often than not, was a slow accumulation of near-misses, wrong fits, and closed doors — with just enough daylight between them to keep going. The door that barely opened This wasn't the first time I was passed over for an opportunity I wanted. In fact, my career at this company felt like one failure after another. When I was a first-year MBA student, I applied for a summer internship at the company where I now work. I was rejected. A few months later, I received an email that felt auto-generated. It was from the company, inviting me to apply for a full-time role. I was confident this was a mistake. They probably didn't filter out summer intern rejections from the target list they sourced from the school. I applied anyway and was accepted. I didn't understand why I wasn't cut out for an internship, but was good enough for a full-time job. I didn't ask. I was happy to have the role. The recruiter let me know that all full-time hires would be receiving introductions to three teams across the company to assess the best mutual fit. I received one introduction. While the role was called a product management role, the real job was to run the team's weekly business reviews. Not quite the product management job I had in mind, but I accepted it anyway. The team I would have never chosen That pseudo-product manager role eventually became a real product manager role. I was promoted to principal product manager with a small team just over three years later. Then, I made a leap to a startup team within the company. I was employee number three on a business that was no more than an idea sketched on a piece of paper. I thought the idea had potential and was excited to be on the ground level to build it. Three months, six hires, and several more papers later, the project was canceled. I was moved to a different team I would never have chosen to join, yet again, working on a product I thought would never find product-market fit. As it turns out, I was wrong. Instead of getting shuttered, the program has scaled tenfold. We expanded the product line from two to four. Customer adoption grew. I was wrong about the product and the team, not because what I saw wasn't real, but because the thing wasn't yet what it was going to be. I spent the next four years on that team. The dud I thought I had been exiled to was the same team that made me a director. What I learned from a career of closed doors There are moments when everyone around you seems to be headed for the exit. Those are often the moments worth staying for. I've learned to run toward fear, shame, and disappointment rather than away from them. What I find is that the people who stay through the hard times earn the trust to do and be more. We get anchored on what we think we should have. I did too, and almost missed what was actually being offered. The job that looks beneath you on paper — running the weekly business review — is often the one that makes you, if you let it. What I had to let go of People talk about resilience like it's armor — something that makes us impervious to pain. That's not how it felt to me. Every failure hurt, but what ultimately helped me get up after every fall wasn't a fancier title, a more glamorous product, or a larger team. It was having the opportunity to make things that people use and love. What I had to be willing to let go of is the path. The door into the company via a summer internship closed, the door into a real product role through post-MBA placement closed, the door to scaled impact through a startup product closed, but the goal remained the same: build things that matter. I was promoted to director six years ago. I now lead larger businesses with larger teams that make a bigger impact on customer lives. How did it feel getting here? About the same as always: like falling forward. Painful stumbles and many detours, but making forward progress nonetheless. Wainwright Yu is a technology executive, mindfulness teacher, and leadership coach who supports neurodivergent individuals as they discover and harness their (often hidden) strengths. articles.title: I went to a private longevity night hosted by Bryan Johnson in San Francisco. I needed a cookie afterward.
articles.summary: When an AI startup announced it was hosting a "private evening" with Bryan Johnson, over 3,000 people applied to get in for just 100 slots.
articles._body: Bryan Johnson cheers on participants as they try to do as many push-ups as possible during a longevity test. Ben Bergman/Business Insider 3,000 people signed up for a "private evening" with biohacker Bryan Johnson. There were only 100 slots. The evening featured breathwork, bioage tests, turmeric juice, and food "guided" by Johnson's chef. I was struck by how many questions came down to people wanting to essentially hack life. The only topic these days that gets people in San Francisco to stop talking about AI is living forever. When Baseten, an AI startup (what else?), announced a few weeks ago, it was hosting a "private evening" with tech entrepreneur and longevity evangelist Bryan Johnson and VC Sarah Guo at its SF office, over 3,000 people applied to get in for just 100 slots. For the uninitiated, Johnson made hundreds of millions selling his payment startup to PayPal and now spends millions a year on a wellness regime that he shares with his 2.7 million Instagram followers. Johnson has been in the news a lot this summer, after he revealed he has autoimmune gastritis, an incurable chronic condition of the stomach. Then, last month, he said, "he might have taken 'this whole longevity thing too far." When I arrived, the registration table was swarmed by people condemned to the waitlist trying to angle their way in. "Don't bother," said the person at the desk. "It's full." Once I squeezed past the crowds, I was handed a color-coded schedule with three stations: Breathwork, Bioage tests, and a Q&A with Dr. Carl Seger , Johnson's lead doctor. "Nothing you measure tonight is a verdict," I was told. "It's a baseline, and every one of these markers can be moved." The Tumeric Elixir Ben Bergman/Business Insider But first, it was time for happy hour! No hors d'oeuvres or wine here. Instead, can I interest you in raw vegetables and mocktails to take the edge off? I opted for a refreshing "Tumeric Elixir" with orange juice, carrot juice, ginger, and tumeric. As soon as I walked in, I noticed everyone seemed overwhelmingly youthful. One tech founder in his fifties told me he felt ancient. So either Johnson's routine is working wonders or this crowd was emblematic of Silicon Valley's "youthquake." I asked an enthusiastic young machine learning engineer who works at Uber why he was there. "Bryan Johnson is just so cool!" he said. But enough chitchat. It was time to get my face scanned to learn my "face age." After a few minutes, a reading popped up. I was in the 80th percentile for wrinkles (which is apparently very good), but my "face age" was older than my real age. The author getting a "face age" scan Ben Bergman/Business Insider Feeling a little dejected, I walked over to the bioage stations, where participants underwent a series of tests, such as grip strength, push-ups, and a one-leg stand, to measure their biological age. Johnson, accompanied by his new guard dog, Katara, strode by, playfully encouraging people to do a few more push-ups. A few feet away, engineers were coding on giant screens. We were in an office after all, not a gym, and the work must go on. Before Johnson's interview, it was time for a dinner "guided" by his personal chef, Tara Amanya. There were box meals with chicken and vegetables, but I opted for the salmon, which was tasty but left me a bit hungry. A salmon dinner "guided" by Bryan Johnson's personal chef Ben Bergman/Business Insider Anything that gets people to exercise more or eat healthier should be commended. Still, I was struck by how many questions throughout the night came down to people wanting easy shortcuts to essentially hack life, as if it were an algorithm to be exploited. Again and again, people kept asking: "What is the  one  thing I can do to live longer?" I kept thinking about my grandparents, who never heard of peptides or biohacking. They drank wine with dinner every night and mostly ate whatever they wanted. They all lived well into their nineties. Sarah Guo from Conviction Capital interviews Bryan Johnson Ben Bergman/Business Insider Johnson is far more self-aware than he can seem on Instagram, and when he was interviewed by Guo to end the evening, he said: "We all know I'm going to die, but it's going to be being hit by a bus or choking on broccoli." "I give you permission to revel in the joy of it," he continued. "That is irony, and my ultimate foe is irony." After the talk ended, I walked back to my hotel and ordered a chocolate chip cookie. Do you have a tip about life in Silicon Valley? Contact reporter Ben Bergman securely on Signal at @BenBergman.11 Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: The feds seized a stake in Anthropic from Sam Bankman-Fried's friends. What happened to the shares?
articles.summary: Sam Bankman-Fried's Anthropic stake was liquidated in bankruptcy court two years ago. His friends' shares went down a different path.
articles._body: Two associates of Sam Bankman-Fried invested in Anthropic. After they were sentenced for fraud, their shares entered a legal black hole. ANGELA WEIS/Getty Images; Tyler Le/BI Sam Bankman-Fried's Anthropic stake was liquidated in bankruptcy court two years ago. The feds seized shares belonging to two co-conspirators, Caroline Ellison and Nishad Singh. The government quietly sold those Anthropic shares last year. It's unclear where the money will go. A little over a year ago, the federal government acquired a stake in Anthropic without paying a penny. The shares were seized from associates of the crypto fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried . From there, they disappeared into a legal black hole. As Anthropic rockets toward what could be the biggest IPO in history , those shares could now be worth billions of dollars. Bankman-Fried's own Anthropic stake was liquidated in the bankruptcy of his failed cryptocurrency exchange. The Anthropic equity owned by Caroline Ellison and Nishad Singh, two associates who invested alongside him, took a different path. The government seized those shares and sold them to existing Anthropic shareholders, according to a person familiar with the sale. It's still unclear whether the proceeds will be paid out to victims of the $11 billion fraud case, or if the feds will just keep the money. It also remains a mystery which investors bought Singh's and Ellison's stock and how much they paid, but Anthropic shares have been on such a dizzying climb that it's likely those investors made a killing on them. Bankman-Fried was convicted in 2023 on fraud and money laundering charges and sentenced to 25 years in prison after the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire. Prosecutors said he used his crypto hedge fund, Alameda Research, to siphon billions of dollars from customers of FTX, his crypto exchange. The story of the crypto criminals' Anthropic shares is a tale with extraordinary elements, including one of the biggest financial frauds in modern history, a messy bankruptcy docket, and a company that experienced one of the fastest appreciations in business history as the world suddenly realized AI's existential importance. An intelligent investment Bankman-Fried, Singh, and Ellison each invested in Anthropic's 2022 Series B funding round. Bankman-Fried bought $500 million worth, which according to court records represented 13.56% of Anthropic at the time. Singh acquired $40 million in shares, and Ellison acquired $10 million in shares, court records reviewed by Business Insider show. The artificial intelligence company's valuation has soared over the past four years. On the secondary market, Anthropic has been valued at $1.5 trillion . It is the most valuable private company in the world, according to Crunchbase . The Anthropic shares purchased by Singh and Ellison could together be worth between $4.17 billion and $5.03 billion today, based on the $965 billion valuation the company announced this May, according to Olav Sorenson, who teaches venture capital strategy at UCLA. Harrison Rolfes, an analyst at PitchBook, put the combined figure at $2.62 billion. If Anthropic went public at a $2 trillion valuation, the shares would be worth about $5.44 billion, Rolfes said. Among Sam Bankman-Fried's many investments was a sizable stake in Anthropic, the AI company that has since soared in value. Bloomberg/Getty Images Four of Bankman-Fried's close friends and executives at his companies pleaded guilty as co-conspirators. Two of them, Singh and Ellison , testified against him. Ellison was the CEO of Alameda Research , which traded and invested funds that belonged to FTX depositors. She was also Bankman-Fried's on-and-off romantic partner. Singh, an FTX executive and early employee, helped hide the commingling of funds between the two companies. After the collapse of FTX, Bankman-Fried's Anthropic shares — which were owned by Clifton Bay, an entity affiliated with Alameda Research — ended up in bankruptcy court along with the other dredged-up remains of his companies. His Anthropic shares were liquidated to pay FTX's creditors. The estate in 2024 sold Bankman-Fried's Anthropic shares to a few dozen buyers for a total of $1.3 billion, more than double what he paid. The largest stake went to an entity affiliated with the United Arab Emirates sovereign wealth fund, bankruptcy court filings show. The feds take a stake in Anthropic As part of their sentences, a judge required Singh and Ellison to forfeit their Anthropic shares, which prosecutors said could be considered proceeds of their crimes. At Singh's sentencing hearing, one of his attorneys, Andrew Goldstein, said Singh purchased his shares before participating in the criminal conspiracy and "he actually may have had a legitimate legal claim" to the shares but agreed to give them up as part of his plea agreement "because it was the right thing to do." Reached for comment for this story, Goldstein told Business Insider that Singh hopes the government is able to quickly distribute proceeds of the sale to FTX victims. An attorney for Ellison declined to comment. Nishad Singh was required to give up his shares of Anthropic as part of his sentence. Bloomberg/Getty Images A federal judge ordered Ellison's and Singh's Anthropic shares to be transferred to the federal government, which took ownership of Ellison's shares in February 2025 and Singh's in April of that year, according to previously unreported court records. Ordinarily, victims of crimes are compensated through a restitution process, which is overseen by courts. But the number of potential FTX victims could be in the millions, prosecutors said in court filings. As a result, the judge ruled, victim compensation would be handled through a process called remission, which is overseen by the Justice Department. During Ellison's sentencing hearing, Justice Department prosecutors told the judge that the DOJ would either set up its own claims administration process to compensate victims, or wo

articles.title: Bosses say Gen Zers aren't ready for work. Whose fault is that?
articles.summary: Every generation of new grads doesn't know how to work. Gen Z has it especially rough.
articles._body: Getty Images; Tyler Le/BI My first internship gave me a simple task: Email a press release to a large list of reporters. I followed the meticulous formatting instructions from a binder, and hit send. Minutes later, a supervisor let me know that I had botched this most basic responsibility. I needed to BCC the list of recipients, something I had neglected to do because in my time in a college classroom, I hadn't learned what BCC meant. It was the kind of rookie mistake I couldn't anticipate and learn only by bumbling through my first office job. For today's young workers, navigating first jobs may become even more complicated. Bosses say Gen Z isn't really workplace ready. Glenn Fogel, CEO of Priceline's parent company Bookings Holdings, has said young workers need more guidance on the norms of the office. Former Whole Foods CEO John Mackey said that young people "don't seem like they want to work." In 2024, a poll of nearly 1,000 business leaders from Intelligent.com found that 75% of companies said some or all of recent grads they hired were "unsatisfactory," and another survey of 800 HR leaders sponsored by Hult International Business School, found that 37% of HR leaders said would prefer to have a robot or AI do a job than hire a recent new grad, while another 30% said they would rather leave the job vacant. "Workplace ready" is a slippery designation that shifts shape by industry or office. Employers hungry for workers who know how to get an ROI on AI have tied their hopes to an ever-growing cohort of AI native Gen Zers entering the workforce. After emphasizing technical skills during the 2010s, they're finding AI can automate some of that work. Communication has become more valuable, just as a generation who had their adolescence marred by COVID and grew up on screens enters the workforce. "What I think colleges need to do — and companies — is first integrate people into what is work: how do you socialize, what is expected of you, and then how can you help me with AI, using AI to help enhance our processes that we have today," says Jason Desentz, chief human resources officer at Toshiba, who sees training young people as a "shared responsibility" between schools and colleges. Desentz also thinks schools should emphasize skills over what many think of as traditional academia. "Can we focus on the stuff that actually matters, and get rid of the fluff?" he says "The question isn't whether colleges should prepare students for careers. They absolutely must," says Lynn Pasquerella, president of the American Association of Colleges and Universities. "It's whether we prepare students for the job that exists today, or give them the kinds of knowledge, skills, competencies, and judgments to navigate a lifetime of work in an economy that's going to continue to change, especially with the rapid proliferation of AI." New grads may never have stepped into the office workplace ready. But today's young workers have a maze with even more twists and turns to navigate. Each generation unlocks a new stigma upon entering the workforce. Gen X bosses saw Millennials as soft and spoiled, Boomer bosses saw Gen Xers as apathetic slackers, and Silent Generation bosses saw Boomers as hippies determined to disrupt the society's morals and norms. The allegations against Gen Z, who embraced Lazy Girl jobs and Quiet Quitting , are just the latest packaging. "Every age group gets that complaint because the transition from school to work is different," says Peter Cappelli, a professor in the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. That transition smooths, and young people grow into jobs just as their parents did. But the professors I spoke to for this story agreed that these new grads are different — they're coming to college without the communication skills typical freshman had in the past. COVID-19 shutdowns disrupted their high school experience. Gen Z has spent more time on screens and less time dating than their predecessors, and just over a third of those ages 16 to 19 worked a summer job this year, a rite of passage that reached a historic high of 58% in 1978, according to the Pew Research Center. They have grown up with parents increasingly involved in school and extracurriculars who have constant connection to their kids, some of which they have maintained throughout college and the early years of their children's careers. A growing number of Americans are questioning the value of a college degree . A 2024 Gallup poll found that just 36% of respondents had a "great deal" of confidence in the higher education system, compared to 57% in 2015. Palantir has offered a pipeline for people to skip college and intern at the company. Stanford dropout Sam Altman recently said he thought four years was too long for college, and that the experience could be dramatically compressed. The professors I spoke to said that if anything, today's college students need more time to develop. Tessa West, a professor of psychology at New York University who a piece for The Wall Street Journal earlier this year titled "A New Lost Generation: Why Gen Z Is Unprepared for the Workplace," says she has noticed freshman have arrived on campus less able to communicate, and with less experience in romantic relationships, debating, or confronting professors. In some ways, college professors now have to build the skills previous students had mastered upon arriving at campus into their coursework. "It falls on us to fix it," West says. "Anyone can learn the technical skills. It's the relational skills." Now add that college students have been handed the keys to Gen AI tools that are altering how people communicate with one another and make it easier to cheat their way to a degree and enter the workforce with neutered critical thinking skills. Headlines about Gen Z in the workforce have sounded alarm bells. The Financial Times reported this spring about a finance firm that pivoted away from STEM graduates toward those with humanities

articles.title: Ukrainians slapped twin AK rifles on a drone with wheels to make a cheap mobile turret
articles.summary: Kyiv has been looking to cheaper assault drones that it can scale rapidly to reduce the risks to its infantry.
articles._body: Two Kalashnikov assault rifles are mounted on a turret to form an assault UGV. Screenshot via X/Brave1 Ukraine has built a drone turret using two Kalashnikov rifles as its main attack option. They're a cheap platform that the country's defense tech incubator, Brave1, says it can scale quickly. It's already been used in combat, with more than 5 units testing it operationally, Brave1 said. A Ukrainian manufacturer developed a roving turret with two Kalashnikov assault rifles for its main armament, as Kyiv aims to build more cheap ground drones to fill dangerous infantry roles. The uncrewed ground vehicle was recently used in combat by the Security Service of Ukraine's Alpha Group special forces to destroy a Russian ambush drone, said the country's defense tech incubator, Brave1, on Thursday. "Why the Kalashnikov? The reason is simple: It's the most widely available small arm across our military units," the incubator wrote in a social media post, adding that using the assault rifle allowed its forces to "rapidly scale" the drones on the front lines. Neither the drone nor the manufacturer was named, though Brave1 said the drone's creator is a member of its platform. The Kalashnikov design was built for a technical brief issued by Brave1. A Ukrainian robot destroys a Russian ambush drone with dual-wielded Kalashnikov rifles — this is the reality on the frontline in Ukraine. A Brave1 member company developed a specialized turret for the Kalashnikov based on our technical brief. It took them less than 6 months to… pic.twitter.com/ocd962Kium — BRAVE1 (@BRAVE1ua) August 27, 2026 More than five Ukrainian units are operationally testing the drone, Brave1 added. Footage of the turret shows the two Kalashnikov rifles mounted closely to each other on a frame attached to a pan-and-tilt gimbal, which in turn rests on a four-wheeled platform. Each rifle appears to be modified behind the grip and trigger guard to remotely receive fire commands, though no other significant tweaks are visible. Notably, Brave1 showed clips of a person manually reloading one of the Kalashnikovs with a box magazine and then racking the bolt, indicating that the turret's current design still requires a soldier nearby to help it stay in a prolonged fight. Ukraine has been developing uncrewed ground vehicles for all manner of tasks, including ground assault, artillery cover, casualty evacuation, mine-clearing, and logistics for years. They've been a major, though not complete, solution for its shortage of soldiers on the front lines and forward areas, which have become saturated with drones and deadly to cross or navigate. The new Kalashnikov turret points to a Ukrainian emphasis on building cheaper, simpler systems to be built quickly for the war. "We are scaling cheap combat UGVs and robotizing the front line to reduce risks to our infantry," Brave1 said in its post. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: Google is getting flak for changing Lake Ontario's name to Lake America
articles.summary: Canadian politicians are also scrubbing government websites that embed Google Maps to ensure the lake is labeled Lake Ontario.
articles._body: Google Maps has changed the name of Lake Ontario for American users. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Google Maps now labels Lake Ontario as Lake America for its US users. The backlash on the internet was swift, with people criticizing Google for the change. Canadian politicians are also scrubbing their government websites that embed Google Maps. Google Maps changed Lake Ontario's name for its American users, and the internet is not happy. On Thursday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario, which straddles the Canadian and US border, to Lake America. The US Geographic Names Information System formally changed the name of the water body. On Sunday, Google said it updates Maps based on official government sources, meaning US users would see "Lake America" while Canadian users would see "Lake Ontario."Users outside these two countries would see "Lake Ontario (Lake America)." The backlash to Google's change was swift. Some users on X called the change "pathetic" and an instance of Google "distributing misinformation." Another said it showed how weak Google was, with how it "bows down to" Trump. Another more creative X user called the tool "Google Craps." The change also got some blowback from Canadian politicians . Stephen Crawford, a member of Ontario's provincial parliament, said some Canadian government websites displayed "Lake America" because they pull map data from Google Maps, an issue the province is fixing. Canadian business news outlet BNN Bloomberg reported that Metrolinx, the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area's public transit network, was among them. "Some Ontario government agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps. Following recent changes by Google, we're actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario," Crawford said in his Sunday post. Crawford added in his post, "As Ontarians, we will always stand up for our province, our identity and the places that define it." When Business Insider checked Metrolinx's website on Sunday evening, the lake was labeled Lake Ontario. Ontario Premier Doug Ford reposted Crawford's post, adding: "Make no mistake: Lake Ontario is and always will be Lake Ontario." In response to a request for comment from Business Insider, a Google spokesperson said that website developers who embed Google Maps on their site can select a region to localize the map, which determines how place names are displayed. "'Lake Ontario' will show when developers have set their region to Canada," the spokesperson said. On the other side of the aisle, the Google Maps change was welcomed by Trump supporters on X, who lauded it. 🚨 LMFAO! Donald Trump is now taking a victory lap after Google Maps CAVES, renames Lake Ontario to Lake America in the app Send it to every Canadian! 🤣 It's Lake America and we're NEVER GOING BACK 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/WgH8kfRQTt — Eric Daugherty (@EricLDaugh) August 30, 2026 Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: Singapore's developer scene was broken, not cracked. Vibe coding fixed it.
articles.summary: AI Tinkerers Singapore has been running demo nights, workshops, and hackathons that draw more than 100 people each time.
articles._body: The AI Engineer Singapore organizer team. AI Engineer Singapore Singapore's tech and hackathon scene dwindled during and after the pandemic. Vibe coding and organic tech collectives have helped bring that excitement back to the city. 65labs' AI hackathon and AIE conference have helped redefine Singapore as an AI hub. When Yong Quan Tan graduated from college in 2023, he was still thinking of himself as a "traditional software engineer." Playing around with OpenAI's GPT -4, which had come out that March, worried him that his developer skills wouldn't be enough to get or keep a job in tech. "I was freaking out. I was like, OK, I have to go for AI events because I have no idea what's going on," he said. "It feels like the asteroid is going to hit the dinosaurs anytime soon." He went looking for somewhere to learn what was happening. In Singapore, where he is based, there wasn't much of an AI scene to find. While Singapore is home to thousands of tech startups, what it lacked, according to the AI builders Business Insider spoke to, was the developer culture associated with hubs like San Francisco, Tel Aviv, and Bengaluru that produced "cracked" engineers — slang for exceptionally talented coders. AI has changed that dramatically. Over the past two years, a collection of grassroots organizers, hackathons, and builder communities has turned Singapore into an unlikely hotbed for people who want to create software. Vibe coding — using natural language to get AI to write software — has lowered the mental and financial cost of building and given almost anyone a ticket into the AI boom. That momentum has given AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic, and scaleups like Cursor and Cognition, an incentive to establish Asia Pacific headquarters in Singapore, adding hundreds of tech and non-tech jobs. No presentation slides For Tan, the turning point came in late 2024, when he came across the Singapore chapter of AI Tinkerers, a San Francisco-based group that hosts AI meetups. The format was deliberately unlike the buttoned-up tech events he was used to. Builders showed each other how they were using the latest AI models to build tools for their daily lives — rough, buggy projects were welcome, while presentation slides were not. Tan was hooked. When Henry Mao, who founded the Singapore chapter of AI Tinkerers, wanted to step away to work full-time on his startup, Tan kept asking to take over. "Henry was like, I've never seen anyone be so persistent. OK, you get it, bro," Tan said, adding that he took over the group last year. Tan presenting at a builder meetup in Singapore. Yong Quan Tan AI Tinkerers Singapore, now called Natives, runs demo nights, workshops, and hackathons focused on everything from voice agents to agentic workflows. Its events regularly draw more than 100 people — a number capped by venue constraints rather than applicant interest, according to Tan. "We were just running events, but then people suddenly started to feel like this could be something that they were a part of, something that they belong to," Tan said. He said two attendees met through the community and went on to cofound an agentic AI startup together. The comeback story AI Tinkerers wasn't the only group noticing the hunger to bring back tech-focused conversations and community. Before the pandemic, Singapore had a buzzing, established tech and hackathon scene, centered on startup incubators like BLOCK71 and backed heavily by universities, government agencies, and corporates like Grab and Amazon. Hackathons spanning consumer tech, blockchain, and smart-city tech routinely drew hundreds of builders, before the scene dwindled during and after COVID. 65labs, a Singapore-based builder collective, entered 2025 with a philosophy of hosting events designed to send attendees home wanting to make something. Its Cursor hackathon in October received more than 1,000 applications and brought hundreds of builders together for 24 hours. Participants shipped nearly 150 working products, including an AI "auntie" that reminds you to take your meds with humor, and a LinkedIn-based dating app that could help you check your compatibility with AMD's Lisa Su. 10 sponsors committed more than $400,000 in resources and support to winning teams. The robot demo room at AIE Singapore 2026. Yong Quan Tan By May 2026, 65labs had helped bring AI Engineer's first Asian conference to Singapore. More than 1,000 people attended the three-day conference backed by companies including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Cursor, Vercel, Cloudflare, and Stripe. Its 92-person speaker roster was filled with founders and experts from the world's biggest AI companies who had flown 16 hours from San Francisco to demo what they're building with AI. A surprise addition to the slate was Singapore's foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan, who spoke about how he uses NanoClaw agents and how he's a "geek" and "tinkerer" himself. Built as a more secure alternative to OpenClaw, NanoClaw agents are lightweight, open-source personal AI assistants that can perform tasks such as answering emails or sorting photos. A common takeaway from the explosion of X and LinkedIn posts that followed the conference was: Don't dismiss Singapore as an AI hub, things are just getting started. Rise of the non-technical founder For Nehal Agrawal, who dis communications AI Engineer, the important part of that recent boom isn't simply that Singapore has more AI events: it's about who feels like they belong at them. When Agrawal graduated in 2024 as a business major, to her, AI was synonymous with ChatGPT. She said that people in research or engineering started learning how to use AI, but as someone non-technical, AI felt "gated." Vibe coding blew a hole through that gate. A speaker hosting AI workshops at AIE Singapore. AI Engineer Singapore At one builder event she attended in early 2026, Agrawal said roughly 1,000 people, ranging from 18-year-olds to people in their 80s, turned up on a Monday night. It's not ju

articles.title: WNBA gameday discussion: Questions for the Minnesota Lynx, Atlanta Dream, Dallas Wings and more before the FIBA World Cup break
articles.summary: It’s the final day of WNBA action before the FIBA World Cup break, with the regular season pausing until Thursday, Sept. 17. Sunday’s games begin with the Minnesota Lynx visiting the Atlanta Dream in a potential playoff preview (3 p.m. ET, NBA TV). Then, the Los Angeles Sparks play the Seattle Storm
articles._body: Olivia Miles and Allisha Gray. | Getty Images It’s the final day of WNBA action before the FIBA World Cup break, with the regular season pausing until Thursday, Sept. 17. Sunday’s games begin with the Minnesota Lynx visiting the Atlanta Dream in a potential playoff preview (3 p.m. ET, NBA TV). Then, the Los Angeles Sparks play the Seattle Storm in what will be Nneka Oguwmike’s final game in Pacific Northwest (5 p.m. ET, WNBA League Pass). The Golden State Valkyries, fresh off a pair of defensive masterclasses on the East Coast, are back out West to face the Portland Fire (7 p.m. ET, WNBA League Pass). Finally, the Dallas Wings will aim to maintain their upward momentum against the Connecticut Sun (8:30 p.m. ET, WNBA League Pass0. With four games on the docket, here’s one question for every matchup. In the comments, be sure to share your answers to these key questions, while also posing your own queries. Are the Dream a real threat to the Lynx? The Dream have enjoyed outlier success against the Lynx in recent seasons. Last year, Atlanta was the only team to take their season series over Minnesota, winning two of the three matchups—including handing the 2025 Lynx their first home loss. This season, the teams have split their two games, although both occurred in May; and while the Dream eked out a one-point win in both teams’ season opener, the Lynx comfortably won the second matchup by 15 points. If the teams were to meet in the playoffs, likely in the second round, is Atlanta a legitimate threat to Minnesota? DeWanna Bonner already settled in with the Atlanta Dream 🙂‍↕️ 🎥 niathmp | Threads pic.twitter.com/VSAidrtRe7 — zavanté 𑣲. (@zavanchy) August 29, 2026 Sunday’s showdown could inspire confidence or doubt in the Dream’s ability to challenge to all-but-official No. 1-seed. With their rebounding prowess, Atlanta can exploit Minnesota’s greatest and most glaring weakness. However, if the Lynx just make their shots, as they often do as the league’s second-best shooting team, the Dream, a bottom-five shooting team from the field and from 3, could struggle to keep up. That Minnesota is a low-turnover team also robs Atlanta, a team that generates their best offense off takeaways, of a potential advantage. While DeWanna Bonner is expected to make her Dream debut on Sunday, the game will not be a full potential playoff preview. Brionna Jones remains sidelined for Atlanta with a leg injury. For Minnesota, Courtney Williams is probable to return from her right foot injury, but Dorka Juhász and Anotonia Delaere already have left for the World Cup, where they’ll be suiting up for Hungary and Belgium, respectively. How will the Storm bid farewell to Nneka? Just five games remain in Nneka Ogwumike’s WNBA career. On Sunday afternoon, she’ll say farewell for the only other WNBA team she knew. Nneka interrupted her 13 seasons in LA with a two-season stint in Seattle, recruited to be part of the first Storm dynasty following the Breanna Stewart era. Seattle, however, was never more than the sum of their parts, not threatening as a contender despite their accumulation of talent. Ogwumike, nevertheless, was as excellent as ever as a Storm, averaging 16.6 points and 7.3 rebounds across her 81 games in green and gold. She also collected two more All-WNBA and All-Star honors in Seattle, along with another All-Defense selection and the 2025 Kim Perrot Sportsmanship Award. Despite her impending retirement, Ogwumike also has been as excellent as ever as of late for the Sparks. On Friday night, she scored a game-high 24 points, in addition to dishing five assists and nabbing four steals, as the Sparks upset the Washington Mystics. Before that, she put up a 27-point and 16-rebound double-double in LA’s close loss to Atlanta. Nneka Ogwumike shined in the @LASparks dub against the Mystics 🌟 24 PTS | 5 AST | 4 STL | 4 REB | 2 3PM | 11/16 FG She also totaled 711 steals in her regular-season career, passing Alana Beard for 4th-most in WNBA history! #WNBASeason30 pic.twitter.com/8pIPH94jUs — WNBA (@WNBA) August 29, 2026 After that win over DC, which included a 17-point comeback, Ogwumike insisted in her postgame interview that her team would continue to “respect” the game, refusing to go through the motions in spite of their elimination from playoff contention. Expect Nneka to bring that same attitude on Sunday, as the Seattle faithful also give her her respect. Will the Golden State juggernaut roll through Rose City? After the Valkyries handed the Sun a 25-point loss on Wednesday, Connecticut play-by-play announcer Brendan Glasheen gave Golden State significant praise on social media. Might have seen the best 40-minute performance (O & D) by a team this year in Golden State last night. Connected defensive team. Statistically great, but 👁️ test… PHEW. Up and close it’s impressive. Dangerous team. If/when Gabby, VB, Salon score/get downhill, title contender. — Brendan Glasheen (@BrendanGlasheen) August 27, 2026 Sounds great, but they were playing the 10-win Sun. Well, on a back-to-back in Brooklyn, the Valkyries held the Liberty to 60 points, securing the season sweep of New York. Now winners of three-straight games, the Valkyries can cruise into the World Cup break on a four-game winning streak, consolidating the growing sense that, despite relying on depth over stardom, this team can, and will, pack the requisite postseason punch. On Sunday, that depth will certainly have the opportunity to shine, as Gabby Williams and Janelle Salaün are off to join the French national team before the World Cup, with Cecilia Zandalisini headed to represent Italy. Development player Miela Sowah will also be participating in the World Cup with the Australian Opals. Yet as they showed in Atlanta on Friday night, and as Bridget Carleton recently told Sue Bird on her Bird’s Eye View podcast, the Fire are not inclined to make things easy on opponents, satisfied to play spoiler through the remainder of the regular season.

articles.title: Why women’s basketball will always love Dolly Parton
articles.summary: This broken nation tormented by anti-intellectualism and a politics of lethargy briefly put all that to the side to commemorate the life of one of the world’s greatest cultural heroines: Dolly Parton. The country music powerhouse and philanthropist passed away at age 80 on Tuesday, Aug. 25. Immediat
articles._body: Dolly Parton. This broken nation tormented by anti-intellectualism and a politics of lethargy briefly put all that to the side to commemorate the life of one of the world’s greatest cultural heroines: Dolly Parton. The country music powerhouse and philanthropist passed away at age 80 on Tuesday, Aug. 25. Immediately, a flood of tributes was unleashed, with politicians, athletes, fellow musicians, actors, other cultural figures and her legion of everyday fans sharing fond feelings and memories about the woman who wore the coat of many colors. Her signature hits “I Will Always Love You”, “9 to 5” and “Jolene” are timeless classics. Dolly’s unquestioned genuineness and unabashed generosity will forever hold a place in the hearts of people around the nation and world. Global icon and humanitarian, Dolly Parton, known to the world as a beloved singer, songwriter, philanthropist, actress, playwright, and author died peacefully today in Nashville, Tennessee. She was 80 years old. Dolly is preceded in death by her beloved husband of 59 years… pic.twitter.com/sBdu2Ssof9 — Dolly Parton (@DollyParton) August 25, 2026 Dolly’s legacy was so big that she intersected with other spaces in the culture beyond her stomping grounds of music and cinema. One of those was women’s basketball. While the sport may not be top of mind when you think of Parton, the celebration of her within the sport will say otherwise. Former University of North Carolina coach Sylvia Hatchell remembers a time when Dolly used the team locker room as her dressing room before a concert when she was head coach of Francis Marion University in South Carolina. Dolly had left a note behind wishing the team luck. Hatchell later credited Dolly’s note as a motivator in their 1982 AIAW Division II national championship win. In February 2024, Lipscomb University, a private Christian college in Nashville, paid homage to Dolly by wearing customized pink rhinestone-accented uniforms patched together by fashion students, who put together an exhibit on campus entitled “Dolly Parton and the Makers: My Life in Rhinestones”. View this post on Instagram In March of this year, Dolly’s high school, Sevier County High School in Sevierville, TN, saw the girls’ basketball team win its first state championship since 2002. Dolly recorded a message to the team celebrating them, telling them, “You girls have really knocked it out of the park. Well, out of court, I guess I should say.” Following Dolly’s passing, WNBA teams participated in the commemoration of the cultural icon, with fans and players alike singing and dancing along to “9 to 5” in the arenas of the Seattle Storm and Las Vegas Aces. The Dallas Wings also amplified and extended the city’s celebration of Parton. @evelynjoyy had me emotional ngl💔 the storm played dolly partons 9 to 5 during a timeout and everyone was dancing. Rip dolly❤️ @seattlestorm #seattlestorm #dollyparton #9to5 #wnba #seattlestormbasketball ♬ original sound – evelyn @LVAces Tribute To #DollyParton Everybody loves DOLLY!!!! Toronto Tempo vs Las Vegas Aces 📍Michelob ULTRA Arena at Mandalay Bay Resort & Casino pic.twitter.com/oelXuOFPyL — Kenya #TheCandyShop (@KenyaTST) August 29, 2026 Working 9-5 🥹🥹🩷 https://t.co/QmB9PoO9mU — Dallas Wings (@DallasWings) August 26, 2026 Other voices in the women’s sports space also have recognized the resonance of Parton within women’s basketball. Over at the Minnesota-focused sports blog Hitting the Hardwood , Kenneth Ward offered a tribute to Parton by assigning every Minnesota Lynx player a Parton song. TOGETHXR co-founder Jessica Robertson wrote a Substack post connecting and celebrating the examples of Dolly and another Tennessee icon: Pat Summitt. It's not too often you connect someone like Dolly Parton to the Minnesota Lynx, but here we are… In celebration of Dolly’s legendary life and seemingly endless catalog of songs, @kennethwardHTX presents to you the Minnesota Lynx, according to Dolly 🩷🏀 https://t.co/eTwr69PbBL — Hitting the Hardwood (@HittingHardwood) August 27, 2026 Two Tennessee girls. One in rhinestones, one in orange. Pat and Dolly left the world with fewer rules about who gets to belong ⭐ Read the full piece by @jesscribe : https://t.co/a48c0APaOY pic.twitter.com/luf2Pvv4hj — TOGETHXR (@togethxr) August 27, 2026 There was nothing that Dolly couldn’t touch that didn’t turn to gold. While she never, by all accounts, hooped it up, she found a home everywhere she went, including women’s basketball. And in this moment where a toxic, uncalled-for culture war is subsuming the sport, the call to get in touch with our own version of Dolly Parton is greater than ever—because she herself wouldn’t put up with this nonsense. She was all about seeing the good in one another, caring for one another, and cheering one another on. In other words, Dolly told us how to do it right. Let’s honor her by doing just that.

articles.title: Interview: Why versatility is the key to Polish forward Lila Banaszak’s basketball career
articles.summary: Lila Banaszak is a 26-year-old and 6-foot-1 forward who plays for the Polish national team and Flammes Carolo Basket in France. She’s also played professionally in Egypt and Spain. Naturally strong, Lila is capable of playing multiple positions, demonstrating a willingness to do whatever is necessar
articles._body: Lila Banaszak prepares to represent Poland in a EuroBasket Women qualifier. | NurPhoto via Getty Images Lila Banaszak is a 26-year-old and 6-foot-1 forward who plays for the Polish national team and Flammes Carolo Basket in France. She’s also played professionally in Egypt and Spain. Naturally strong, Lila is capable of playing multiple positions, demonstrating a willingness to do whatever is necessary for her team to win. Banaszak recently spoke to Swish Appeal about being a pro, traveling and switching teams while having a dog, playing against adults while still in high school and maybe one day joining the WNBA. Here are a few highlight from our conversation: On attending the Polish Basketball Federation academy: I think the school is not that popular now. People have had their own ways to be successful and build careers, but in my day that was the only basketball school we had. It was ran by the national federation and had good coaches, who could spend time with you on individual skills. For me, being from a small city, there was no other way to get better than going to this kind of school and, to be honest, I never expected that I’d be going there because I didn’t even know about it. Basketball was never a thing for me until they invited me. When they sent a [recruitment] letter to my family, I was on the national under-15 team. We woke up before 7 a.m., had breakfast and at 7:15 a.m. we already had some classes. Then we had practice, then lunch, then classes and then practice. From 7 a.m. till 8, sometimes 9 p.m., we were working, [constantly] doing stuff. In some evenings you had maybe one, two hours to study or take care of yourself, and that was it. On playing professionally in Egypt: There were not a lot of fans in attendance, but our games were on public TV and I know that a lot of people were watching our games. It was thousands of people. I think it’s about the culture. They don’t have much money to attend games, so people don’t come to the arenas but they watch them on TV. This allows [women’s basketball] to be everywhere. The level of basketball is hard to describe because when you go there. There’s no organization, there’s nothing. But at the same time, those girls know how to play basketball. A special thank you to Tomasz Matyskiewicz of SPORTFORUM Agency for arranging the interview.

articles.title: WNBA gameday discussion: Don’t let the Phoenix Mercury’s struggles allow you to forget that Kahleah ‘Freaking’ Copper is still freaking good
articles.summary: KFC has been cooking. This season, Kahleah “Freaking” Copper has six 30-pieces, with the latest coming on Thursday night, when, a night before her 32nd birthday, she scored a sizzling 35 points. Yet, it also was the the fourth time this season that one of her gun-slinging games of 30 or more points
articles._body: Kahleah Copper. | Getty Images KFC has been cooking. This season, Kahleah “Freaking” Copper has six 30-pieces, with the latest coming on Thursday night, when, a night before her 32nd birthday, she scored a sizzling 35 points. Yet, it also was the the fourth time this season that one of her gun-slinging games of 30 or more points came in a loss, as the Phoenix Mercury fell to the Washington Mystics, their fourth-straight loss. Along the way, she also scored her 2,000th point in a Mercury uniform, becoming the fastest Phoenix player ever—yes, faster than Diana Taurasi —to reach that milestone. SHE'S NOT DONE 🚨 31 PTS & counting for Kahleah Copper! She reaches 30+ PTS for the 6th time this season and 17th time in her career! https://t.co/OaNXAm1Ktc pic.twitter.com/a29emWUCzF — WNBA (@WNBA) August 28, 2026 "Shoutout to X-FACTOR, I love y'all so much. I let y'all know last minute… but y'all still showed up, showed out… I was glad that X-FACTOR got to be a part of that because they're a big part of our organization and us having success." Kahleah Copper APPRECIATED all of those… pic.twitter.com/bKshXteaO9 — PHNX Mercury (@PHNX_Mercury) August 28, 2026 That’s the KFC conundrum. Copper is production and prolific as ever, capable of pouring in points from all over the floor. And yet, the Mercury are the WNBA’s most disappointing team, following up a trip to the 2025 WNBA Finals with an early elimination from playoff contention. Early this season, however, Copper looked like the culprit for Phoenix’s woes. Copper was shooting incredibly inefficiently. It took until her 14th game of the season—her career-high 41-point outburst in her bucket-getting duel with now-teammate Kelsey Plum—for Copper to shoot better than 50 percent from the field in a game. Over those first 13 games, she only creeped over 40 percent from the field once. Only her ability to generate trips to the foul line stabilized her scoring output. That 41-point night, in fact, was the turning point. Since then, she’s converted less than 40 percent of her shots just four times. That’s the Kah we know! Her pre-All-Star numbers of 20.5 points on 42.8 percent shooting and 27.5 percent from 3 have elevated to 23.4 points per game on 48.6 percent shooting with a 36.2 percent clip from 3. That progress makes her All-Star selection, as she was a somewhat questionable substitution choice at the time, seem routine. One more time for this 5x All-Star ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ pic.twitter.com/dJSN0uEOZA — Phoenix Mercury (@PhoenixMercury) July 26, 2026 But Copper’s reemergence as one of the more lethal scorers in the WNBA has done little lift Phoenix out of their season-long malaise. Just two games before she ignited for 35 points on Washington, she doused the Atlanta Dream for 38 points, hitting nearly 62 percent of all her shot attempts—in another loss. Individual offensive excellence cannot compensate for poor roster construction. The Mercury, after compiling an effective supporting cast of unheralded players last season, seemed to get a bit too overconfident in their ability to excavate adequate contributions from older or unproven players, failing to surround with Copper and Alyssa Thomas with enough two-way talent. Their last-ditch effort—a midseason trade for Plum that required the organization to sacrifice what will be a lottery pick—also has fallen flat, as Plum has been healthy for just five games. Her absence has robbed the X Factor of the opportunity to at least enjoy some scoring fireworks from the Copper-Plum backcourt. But, there is an upcoming temporary solve for the Copper conundrum: the FIBA World Cup. One week out from the #FIBAWWC ! 🏆 🇺🇸 #USABWNT 7️⃣ @kahleahcopper pic.twitter.com/vO289fRncj — USA Basketball (@usabasketball) August 28, 2026 While WNBA Kah is special, Team USA Kah is really special . And unlike in Phoenix this season, she’ll be part of a roster that will amplify the impact of her scoring prowess, something she proved without a doubt in the 2024 Olympic gold medal game, famously inspiring a succinct stamp of approval from A’ja Wilson. @sluggahjells3 @A’ja Wilson describes @Kahleah Copper ’s performance in the Olympic final @USA Basketball win over France 🥇 to @ZoraStephenson 🤣🤣🤣🤣🤣 #Tiktok #AjaWilson #KahleahCooper #WNBA #Funny #Philly #Philadelphia #Paris #France #Basketball #Ball #Sports #Sport #WomenSports #2024 #Paris2024 #Sunday #Weekend #August #Summer #GoodTimes #Quote #Viral #LMAO #BLM #BlackLivesMatter #BlackGirlMagic ♬ original sound – SluggahJells3 Her speed, always dangerous, acquires extra potency when she dons the red, white and blue, making her the perfect complementary weapon in lineups organized around Team USA’s foundational duo of Wilson and Breanna Stewart. In all the sure to come conversations about the rotations Team USA head coach Kara Lawson should (or shouldn’t) deploy in Berlin, it would be wise not to forget Kah. I expect her to come through in a big moment or two as Team USA marches toward World Cup gold. First, she and the Mercury finish out their pre-World Cup schedule with a visit from the Toronto Tempo, another team aimlessly trudging through the end of the regular season (10 p.m. ET, WNBA League Pass). Copper is listed as probable to play with a tweaked left ankle, while Plum is out due to the management of her left leg issue. What do you expect from Kah, first on Saturday and then in Berlin? Can she cook up another 30-ball to give the Mercury a feel-good win? For Team USA, do you see her emerging as a key player? Share all your Copper thoughts, as well as some appreciation, in the comments.

articles.title: How Beyond the Game Health is already prioritizing athlete wellness for WNBA All-Star 2027
articles.summary: The 2027 WNBA All-Star Game coming to the Bay Area is a testament to what the Golden State Valkyries have built in such a short time… a passionate fanbase, sellout energy, and a community that has embraced women’s basketball at scale. — Zaileen Janmohamed, CEO, Bay Area Host Committee For former ath
articles._body: WNBA All-Star 2027 will be in San Francisco. | NBAE via Getty Images The 2027 WNBA All-Star Game coming to the Bay Area is a testament to what the Golden State Valkyries have built in such a short time… a passionate fanbase, sellout energy, and a community that has embraced women’s basketball at scale. — Zaileen Janmohamed, CEO, Bay Area Host Committee For former athlete and Bay Area resident Shamekka Marty, the announcement that the Golden State Valkyries will host WNBA All-Star 2027 in San Francisco means more than another major sporting event coming to her city.
